title: Paediatric Constipation: Causes, Diagnosis, and Management
subject: Paediatrics
summary: Constipation in children is defined by reduced stool frequency, volume, or hardness. It can be caused by functional issues, diet, or underlying medical conditions. Management focuses on lifestyle changes, laxatives, and addressing the root cause.

sections.p: Constipation is defined as infrequent stools, hard stools, or a reduced volume of stools. Diagnosis in children often relies on clinical history and physical examination, using criteria like the Rome IV criteria.

sections.p: Severity is typically assessed based on symptom duration, frequency, and impact on the child's quality of life. Chronic constipation is defined as lasting for at least 2 months.
b: Mild: Intermittent symptoms, easily managed
Moderate: Persistent symptoms, requiring regular treatment
Severe: Long-standing, difficult-to-treat symptoms with significant impact

sections.p: Management involves education, dietary modifications, disimpaction if needed, and maintenance therapy with laxatives. Addressing behavioural factors is crucial for long-term success.
b: Education: Explain the condition to child and family.
Dietary changes: Increase fibre and fluid intake.
Disimpaction: Oral or rectal agents to clear impacted stool.
Maintenance therapy: Osmotic laxatives (e.g., polyethylene glycol) are preferred for long-term use.
Behavioural therapy: Scheduled toilet sitting, positive reinforcement.

sections.p: Constipation can be mistaken for other conditions that cause abdominal pain or reduced stool output.
b: Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS): Often presents with alternating diarrhoea and constipation, and abdominal pain.
Gastroenteritis: Typically presents with acute diarrhoea and vomiting, not chronic constipation.
Intestinal obstruction: Presents with more acute, severe symptoms like vomiting and distension.

sections.p: Normal investigation results do not always exclude significant constipation, and some symptoms can be misleading.
b: Normal abdominal X-ray: May not show mild faecal loading that is clinically significant.
Absence of encopresis: Does not rule out constipation, as some children withhold stools without soiling.
Child reporting 'normal' stools: May refer to frequency rather than consistency or ease of passage.

faq.q: What is the most common cause of constipation in children?
faq.a: Functional constipation, related to diet, withholding behaviour, and toilet training, is the most common cause.

faq.q: When should I worry about constipation in my child?
faq.a: Worry if there is failure to thrive, vomiting, severe abdominal pain, blood in stool, or if the baby hasn't passed meconium in 48 hours.

exam: A 5-year-old child presents with a 3-month history of infrequent, hard stools and occasional soiling. How would you assess this child at the bedside? — History (frequency, consistency, pain, withholding, diet, fluid intake, toilet training, family history), examination (abdominal distension, palpation for faecal loading, perianal inspection, digital rectal exam if appropriate).

What are the Rome IV criteria for functional constipation in children? — Two or more of the following occurring at least once per week for at least one month: <2 defecations per week, >1 episode of faecal incontinence per week, history of retentive posturing, history of painful or hard stools, large faecal mass in rectum, large diameter stools that may obstruct the toilet.

A child has severe constipation with faecal impaction. What is the initial management step? — Disimpaction, using oral laxatives (e.g., polyethylene glycol) or rectal therapy (e.g., enemas) to clear the impacted stool.

What is the difference between functional constipation and Hirschsprung's disease? — Functional constipation is a motility disorder without an anatomical or neurological defect, while Hirschsprung's disease is a congenital absence of ganglion cells in the distal bowel, leading to a lack of peristalsis.

Why are stimulant laxatives generally avoided for long-term management of paediatric constipation? — They can cause cramping, electrolyte disturbances, and dependency, and are less effective for long-term management compared to osmotic laxatives.

What are the potential complications of untreated chronic constipation in children? — Faecal impaction, faecal incontinence (encopresis), urinary tract infections, rectal prolapse, abdominal pain, poor appetite, and psychosocial distress.

How can you differentiate between overflow incontinence (encopresis) and true faecal incontinence? — Overflow incontinence is due to a large, impacted stool mass that leaks around. True incontinence may be related to behavioural issues or neurological problems and is not necessarily associated with impaction.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: A thorough history and physical examination are crucial for differentiating functional constipation from organic causes and assessing severity. Focus on symptom characteristics, associated features, and potential red flags.
b: Onset and duration of constipation: Was it since birth (suggests Hirschsprung's) or later in infancy/childhood?
Stool characteristics: Frequency, consistency (use Bristol Stool Chart), size (e.g., large diameter stools), pain during defecation, blood in stool.
Associated symptoms: Abdominal pain (location, character, relation to defecation), distension, nausea, vomiting, poor appetite, weight loss, urinary symptoms (e.g., enuresis).
Stool withholding behaviour: Posturing (e.g., standing on tiptoes, crossing legs, hiding), refusal to use toilet, fear of defecation.
Dietary history: Fibre intake (fruits, vegetables, whole grains), fluid intake, consumption of constipating foods (e.g., excessive dairy).
Toilet training history: Age of training, any difficulties or negative experiences.
Medication history: Current and recent medications, including over-the-counter drugs and traditional remedies.
Developmental history: Milestones, neurological concerns (e.g., hypotonia, spina bifida signs).
Family history: Constipation, Hirschsprung's disease, coeliac disease.
Impact on quality of life: School attendance, social activities, emotional well-being.

t.b: Look for signs of chronic illness, malnutrition (wasted limbs, poor growth), pallor, abdominal distension, visible peristalsis (suggests obstruction), or a palpable fecal mass.

Palpate for tenderness, masses (especially a doughy, irregular mass in the left lower quadrant consistent with a fecaloma), organomegaly. A palpable fecal mass indicates significant stool retention. This cannot tell you the exact composition or consistency of the mass.

Assess for tympany (gas) or dullness (stool, fluid). Dullness over the left lower quadrant can support the presence of a fecal mass. This cannot definitively differentiate stool from other masses or fluid.

Listen for bowel sounds. Normal, increased, or decreased sounds can provide clues to bowel activity. Absent bowel sounds suggest paralytic ileus or complete obstruction. This cannot pinpoint the exact location or cause of obstruction.

Look for anal fissures (often a consequence of painful defecation), haemorrhoids, skin tags, perianal excoriation (from soiling), or an anteriorly displaced anus. This cannot rule out internal pathology or assess sphincter tone.

Assess for presence and consistency of stool in the rectum (hard, large fecal mass), anal sphincter tone (normal, increased, decreased), presence of an anal wink reflex (S2-S4 nerve integrity), and any anatomical abnormalities. sections.p: Diagnosis of functional constipation in children is primarily clinical, based on the Rome IV criteria. Severity is assessed by symptom duration, frequency, impact on quality of life, and presence of fecal impaction.
b: 1. Two or fewer defecations in the toilet per week.
2. At least one episode of fecal incontinence per week.
3. History of retentive posturing or excessive voluntary stool retention.
4. History of painful or hard bowel movements.
5. History of large diameter stools that may obstruct the toilet.
6. Presence of a large fecal mass in the rectum on physical examination.
Staging/Severity Assessment:
Mild: Intermittent symptoms, easily managed with dietary changes and occasional laxatives. No significant impact on daily life or fecal impaction.
Moderate: Persistent symptoms requiring regular laxative use. May have occasional fecal incontinence or mild abdominal discomfort. Some impact on quality of life.

Severe: Long-standing, difficult-to-treat symptoms with significant impact on quality of life, school attendance, and social activities. Often associated with chronic fecal impaction and frequent fecal incontinence (encopresis). May involve significant abdominal pain and distension.

Fecal Impaction: Defined by the presence of a large, hard stool mass in the rectum or colon that cannot be passed voluntarily. Failure to pass stool for >1 week in a child >2 years, especially with other symptoms like abdominal pain or soiling, should raise suspicion of impaction. Confirmed by DRE or abdominal X-ray.

sections.p: It is crucial to differentiate functional constipation from organic causes, as the management strategies differ significantly. Red flags in the history and examination should prompt investigation for organic conditions.

sections.p: Management of paediatric constipation focuses on disimpaction, maintenance, and prevention of recurrence, with a strong emphasis on behavioural and dietary modifications alongside pharmacotherapy.
b: Disimpaction: For children with fecal impaction, the initial step is disimpaction. This typically involves high-dose oral osmotic laxatives (e.g., polyethylene glycol, lactulose) given over several days until a large volume of soft stool is passed. Rectal interventions (e.g., enemas) may be considered in severe cases or if oral therapy is ineffective, but are generally less pre

Maintenance Therapy: After successful disimpaction, long-term maintenance therapy is crucial to prevent recurrence. This involves daily use of osmotic laxatives (e.g., polyethylene glycol, lactulose) at a dose sufficient to ensure regular passage of soft, pain-free stools. The goal is 1-2 soft bowel movements per day. This phase can last for several months to years.

Dietary and Lifestyle Modifications: Alongside laxative therapy, education on adequate fluid intake and a high-fibre diet (fruits, vegetables, whole grains) is essential. Encourage regular physical activity. Establish a regular toilet routine, encouraging the child to sit on the toilet for 5-10 minutes after meals, even if they don't feel the urge, to promote a conditioned refl

Behavioural Interventions: Address stool withholding behaviours through positive reinforcement and reward systems. Involve parents in understanding the child's fears and anxieties related to defecation. Psychological support may be beneficial for children with significant behavioural issues or encopresis.

When to Escalate or Refer: If constipation persists despite optimal dosing of osmotic agents for 2-4 weeks, or if there are red flags (e.g., poor growth, recurrent abdominal pain, blood in stool, abnormal neurological signs), consider adding a stimulant laxative (e.g., senna, bisacodyl) for short periods or referring to a paediatric gastroenterologist or surgeon to rule out org

Monitoring: Regular follow-up is necessary to assess stool frequency and consistency, abdominal pain, soiling episodes, and adherence to treatment. Adjust laxative doses as needed to achieve soft, regular stools. Gradually taper laxatives only after several months of symptom-free bowel movements and established healthy bowel habits.

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Understanding the common adverse effects and interactions of laxatives is crucial for safe and effective management of paediatric constipation.
b: Osmotic Laxatives (e.g., Polyethylene Glycol, Lactulose): Common side effects include abdominal bloating, flatulence, and mild abdominal cramps, especially at the start of treatment or with higher doses. Diarrhoea can occur if the dose is too high; reduce the dose. Electrolyte imbalances are rare with standard use but can occur with excessive doses or in vulnerable patients. En

Stimulant Laxatives (e.g., Senna, Bisacodyl): These can cause abdominal cramps and pain due to their direct action on the intestinal wall. Long-term, continuous use is generally avoided in children due to concerns about dependency and potential damage to the colonic nerves, though this is debated. Use for short periods or intermittently when osmotic agents are insufficient afte

Mineral Oil: While historically used, mineral oil is generally discouraged in children due to the risk of aspiration pneumonia, especially in younger children or those with swallowing difficulties. It can also interfere with the absorption of fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K).

Drug Interactions: Laxatives can affect the absorption of other medications by altering gut transit time. For example, some laxatives may reduce the absorption of oral contraceptives or certain antibiotics. Always review the child's full medication list.

sections.p: Untreated or poorly managed chronic constipation can lead to significant physical and psychological complications, necessitating prompt escalation of care.
b: Faecal Impaction: This is a common complication where a large, hard mass of stool accumulates in the rectum and/or colon, leading to partial or complete obstruction. It often presents with abdominal pain, distension, and paradoxical 'overflow' soiling (encopresis). Failure to pass stool for >1 week in a child >2 years, especially with other symptoms, should raise suspicion.

Encopresis (Faecal Incontinence): Involuntary passage of stool, often liquid stool, around a retained faecal mass. This can lead to significant social and psychological distress for the child and family, including shame, low self-esteem, and social isolation. It requires comprehensive management including disimpaction, maintenance, and behavioural therapy.

Anal Fissures and Haemorrhoids: Straining to pass hard stools can cause tears in the anal mucosa (fissures), leading to pain, bleeding, and a vicious cycle of withholding due to fear of pain. Chronic straining can also contribute to the development of haemorrhoids. Bright red rectal bleeding should prompt examination for fissures or haemorrhoids.

Urinary Tract Infections (UTIs) and Enuresis: A distended rectum filled with stool can compress the bladder, leading to incomplete emptying, urinary stasis, and increased risk of UTIs. It can also contribute to daytime or nocturnal enuresis (bedwetting).

Poor Growth and Appetite: Chronic constipation can cause abdominal discomfort, bloating, and early satiety, leading to reduced food intake and potentially poor weight gain or growth faltering. This is a red flag for underlying issues or severe, prolonged constipation.

Psychological Impact: Chronic constipation and encopresis can severely impact a child's quality of life, leading to anxiety, depression, behavioural problems, and difficulties at school and with peers. Referral to child psychology or counselling services may be necessary.

When to Escalate: Persistent symptoms despite adequate treatment, presence of red flags (e.g., poor growth, recurrent abdominal pain, blood in stool, abnormal neurological signs, bilious vomiting, absent bowel sounds, 'bird-beak' sign on imaging), or suspicion of organic causes (e.g., Hirschsprung's disease, spinal cord abnormalities) warrant urgent referral to a paediatric gas

sections.p: Several systemic conditions, medications, and environmental factors can complicate the presentation, diagnosis, and management of constipation in children.
b: Malnutrition: Children with malnutrition, particularly severe acute malnutrition, may have reduced gut motility and altered gut flora, predisposing them to constipation. Re-feeding syndrome can also impact bowel function. Management must be integrated with nutritional rehabilitation.

Neurological Disorders: Conditions like cerebral palsy, spina bifida, or other spinal cord abnormalities can impair bowel innervation and muscle coordination, leading to severe neurogenic constipation. These often require more aggressive and long-term management strategies, including regular bowel regimens and sometimes surgical interventions.

Endocrine Disorders: Hypothyroidism can cause constipation due to decreased gut motility. Diabetes mellitus can lead to autonomic neuropathy affecting bowel function. Screening for these conditions is important in children with unexplained chronic constipation.

Medications: Certain medications commonly used in children can cause constipation as a side effect, including opioids (e.g., for pain management), anticholinergics (e.g., some antihistamines, antispasmodics), certain antiepileptics, and iron supplements. Reviewing the medication list is crucial.

HIV/TB: Children with HIV may experience constipation due to opportunistic infections, side effects of antiretroviral therapy, or autonomic neuropathy. TB can cause abdominal pain and altered bowel habits, though constipation is less common than diarrhoea. These conditions can complicate assessment and require careful consideration.

Dietary Factors: Low fibre intake and inadequate fluid intake are common contributors to functional constipation. Cultural dietary practices and food availability in low-resource settings can significantly influence these factors. Education on accessible high-fibre foods is important.

Psychological Factors: Stress, anxiety, and trauma can exacerbate constipation or contribute to stool withholding. Children experiencing abuse or neglect may present with constipation as a somatic symptom. A holistic approach is essential.

sections.p: Constipation management requires tailored approaches for specific populations, considering their unique physiological and environmental contexts.
b: Infants: Constipation in infants (especially exclusively breastfed) is rare and often suggests an underlying organic cause (e.g., Hirschsprung's disease, anal stenosis). 'Grunting baby syndrome' is not constipation. Management involves careful history, examination, and sometimes formula changes or very gentle osmotic laxatives under medical supervision. Never use stimulant laxa

Children with Disabilities: Children with developmental delays or physical disabilities may have difficulty communicating symptoms, accessing toilets, or performing self-care. They often require highly structured bowel regimens, adapted toilet facilities, and caregiver education. Neurogenic constipation is common in this group.

Low-Resource Settings: Access to appropriate laxatives (especially polyethylene glycol), diagnostic tools (e.g., anorectal manometry, biopsy for Hirschsprung's), and specialist care may be limited. Emphasis shifts to dietary modifications using locally available foods, adequate hydration, and basic osmotic agents (e.g., lactulose) if available. Education of caregivers on red fl

Adolescents: Psychological factors and body image concerns can significantly impact adherence to treatment and willingness to discuss bowel habits. Privacy and a non-judgmental approach are crucial. Education on healthy lifestyle choices and addressing underlying anxieties are key.

Children with Chronic Illnesses: Those with conditions like cystic fibrosis, coeliac disease, or inflammatory bowel disease may have constipation as part of their disease presentation or due to medication side effects. Management needs to be integrated into their overall care plan, often requiring specialist input.

Large fecal mass in rectum on DRE: a Rome IV criterion for functional constipation.
Stool size >2.5 cm: a Rome IV criterion for functional constipation.

vivas.q: What are the key history questions to ask when evaluating a child with constipation?
vivas.a: Key questions include: onset and duration of symptoms, stool frequency and consistency (use Bristol Stool Chart if possible), presence of pain during defecation, stool size, presence of fecal soiling (encopresis), dietary habits (fluid and fiber intake), toilet training history, any associated symptoms (abdominal pain, distension, poor appetite, weight loss), and previous treatments.

vivas.q: Describe the physical examination steps for a child presenting with constipation.
vivas.a: General observation for distress, growth parameters (weight, height). Abdominal examination: inspection for distension, visible peristalsis; palpation for tenderness, palpable fecal masses (especially in left lower quadrant), organomegaly. Perianal inspection for fissures, skin tags, signs of abuse. Digital rectal examination (DRE) if indicated: assess anal tone, presence and consistency of stool in the rectum, exclude anatomical abnormalities.

vivas.q: A child has severe constipation with faecal impaction. What is the initial management step?
vivas.a: The initial management step for severe constipation with fecal impaction is disimpaction. This typically involves high doses of osmotic laxatives, such as polyethylene glycol, administered orally over several days until the impaction is cleared. In some cases, rectal enemas may be considered, but oral therapy is generally preferred.

vivas.q: What is the difference between functional constipation and Hirschsprung's disease?
vivas.a: Functional constipation is typically acquired, often related to diet, withholding, or painful defecation, and is characterized by normal innervation of the bowel. Hirschsprung's disease is a congenital condition caused by the absence of ganglion cells in a segment of the distal bowel, leading to a functional obstruction and typically presenting with symptoms from birth or early infancy, often with a history of delayed meconium passage.

vivas.q: Why are stimulant laxatives generally avoided for long-term management of paediatric constipation?
vivas.a: Stimulant laxatives are generally avoided for long-term management due to concerns about potential dependency, damage to colonic nerve plexuses with prolonged use, and the risk of electrolyte imbalances. They are typically reserved for short-term use or when osmotic agents alone are insufficient after optimal dosing and adherence.

vivas.q: What are the potential complications of untreated chronic constipation in children?
vivas.a: Potential complications include fecal impaction, encopresis (fecal soiling), anal fissures, haemorrhoids, recurrent abdominal pain, urinary tract infections (due to bladder compression), poor appetite, psychological distress, and significant impact on quality of life and school performance.

vivas.q: How can you differentiate between overflow incontinence (encopresis) and true faecal incontinence?
vivas.a: Overflow incontinence (encopresis) is typically associated with chronic constipation and fecal impaction, where liquid stool leaks around a hard, retained fecal mass. True fecal incontinence, in contrast, is the involuntary passage of stool in the absence of impaction, often due to underlying neurological or anatomical issues affecting sphincter control.

vivas.q: List and explain the management strategies and red flags for gastrointestinal discomforts including constipation and haemorrhoids.
vivas.a: Management for constipation involves disimpaction (if present), maintenance therapy with osmotic laxatives, dietary modifications (increased fiber and fluid), behavioral interventions (toilet training, regular toilet sitting), and addressing associated psychological factors. For haemorrhoids, management includes stool softeners, increased fiber, topical creams, and rarely, surgical intervention. Red flags for GI discomfort include weight loss, rectal bleeding (not due to fissure), severe abdominal pain, delayed meconium passage, persistent vomiting, fever, and failure to thrive, suggesting organic causes.

vivas.q: What are the red flags for organic causes of constipation in children?
vivas.a: Red flags include: onset of constipation in the first month of life, delayed passage of meconium (>48 hours), failure to thrive, abdominal distension with vomiting, ribbon-like stools, absent anal wink reflex, sacral dimple or hair tuft, abnormal lower limb neurological examination, blood in stool (not from fissure), and severe abdominal pain.

vivas.q: When is a digital rectal examination (DRE) indicated in a child with constipation?
vivas.a: DRE is indicated if there are red flags for organic causes, suspicion of fecal impaction, or if the diagnosis of functional constipation is unclear after history and abdominal examination. It helps assess anal tone, presence and consistency of stool in the rectum, and exclude anatomical abnormalities.

vivas.q: What is the role of dietary modification in the management of paediatric constipation?
vivas.a: Dietary modification involves increasing fluid intake and dietary fiber. This includes encouraging water, fruit juices (e.g., prune, apple), and incorporating fiber-rich foods like fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and legumes. However, diet alone is often insufficient for established constipation and should be combined with laxative therapy.

vivas.q: What is the 'stool-holding sign' and what does it indicate?
vivas.a: The 'stool-holding sign' refers to behavioral manifestations of stool withholding, such as standing on tiptoes, rocking back and forth, crossing legs, or hiding in a corner. It indicates that the child is actively trying to suppress the urge to defecate, often due to fear of painful bowel movements.

vivas.q: What investigations might be considered for a child with suspected organic constipation?
vivas.a: Investigations depend on the suspected cause. They may include thyroid function tests (for hypothyroidism), serum electrolytes and calcium, abdominal X-ray (for fecal impaction or dilated bowel loops), barium enema (for Hirschsprung's disease), anorectal manometry (to assess rectoanal inhibitory reflex in Hirschsprung's), or rectal biopsy (definitive diagnosis of Hirschsprung's).

mcqs.q: A 55‑year‑old man with a history of chronic constipation presents with abdominal distension, absent bowel sounds and no flatus passage for 24 hours. The most likely underlying problem is:
mcqs.e: Absent bowel sounds and no flatus passage in the context of abdominal distension and chronic constipation suggest paralytic ileus, a functional obstruction.

mcqs.q: A 70-year-old man presents with acute colicky abdominal pain, absolute constipation, and abdominal distension. A computed tomography scan shows a 'bird-beak' sign and a massively dilated sigmoid colon. What is the definition of the most likely underlying problem?
o: A functional paralysis of the bowel without mechanical obstruction.
A blockage of the bowel lumen by hardened stool.
Twisting of a loop of intestine around its mesentery, resulting in obstruction and ischemia.
Inflammation of diverticula in the colon.
mcqs.e: The 'bird-beak' sign and massively dilated sigmoid colon are classic findings for sigmoid volvulus, which is a twisting of the bowel.

mcqs.q: A 45-year-old man who underwent an appendectomy three years ago presents with crampy abdominal pain, vomiting, and absolute constipation. A physical barrier preventing intestinal contents from passing is identified. What is the most likely underlying problem?
mcqs.e: Previous abdominal surgery (appendectomy) is a common risk factor for adhesive small bowel obstruction, which presents with crampy pain, vomiting, and absolute constipation due to a physical barrier.

mcqs.q: A 60-year-old woman presents with acute abdominal pain and absolute constipation following major abdominal surgery. Imaging shows dilated loops of bowel throughout the abdomen with no transition point or physical barrier. What is the most likely underlying problem?
mcqs.e: Post-operative acute abdominal pain, absolute constipation, and dilated bowel loops without a mechanical obstruction (no transition point or physical barrier) are characteristic of paralytic ileus.

mcqs.q: A 68-year-old man presents with progressive abdominal distension, constipation, weight loss, and blood in the stool. Colonoscopy reveals a lesion causing large-bowel obstruction. What is the most common cause of large-bowel obstruction in this age group?
mcqs.e: In an elderly patient with progressive symptoms, weight loss, and rectal bleeding, colorectal carcinoma is the most common cause of large-bowel obstruction.

cases.v: A 3-year-old girl is brought to the clinic by her mother with a 6-month history of infrequent bowel movements (typically once every 5-7 days), which are large and hard. She often cries during defecation and sometimes hides behind furniture, straining. Her appetite has decreased, and she occasionally has small streaks of blood on her stool. On examination, she is otherwise well, with a distended but soft abdomen, and a palpable doughy mass in the left lower quadrant. Perianal inspection reveals a small anal fissure.

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis and what criteria support it?
qs.a: The most likely diagnosis is functional constipation. This is supported by Rome IV criteria: infrequent stools (<2/week), painful/hard bowel movements, retentive posturing (hiding and straining), and a palpable large fecal mass in the rectum/abdomen. The anal fissure is a common complication of passing hard stools.

qs.q: Outline the initial management plan for this child.
qs.a: The initial management involves disimpaction (if confirmed by DRE or X-ray) using high-dose oral osmotic laxatives (e.g., polyethylene glycol) until the impaction is cleared. This is followed by maintenance therapy with osmotic laxatives, dietary modifications (increased fluids and fiber), behavioral interventions (regular toilet sitting after meals), and treatment of the anal fissure (e.g., topical anaesthetic, stool softeners).

qs.q: What red flags would prompt you to investigate for an organic cause?
qs.a: Red flags that would prompt investigation for an organic cause include: onset of constipation in the first month of life, delayed passage of meconium, failure to thrive (though she has decreased appetite, her growth is not explicitly stated as poor), ribbon-like stools (though her stools are large and hard), absent anal wink, sacral abnormalities, or persistent vomiting.

cases.v: A 6-month-old infant presents with a history of chronic constipation since birth, characterized by infrequent, hard stools and significant abdominal distension. The mother reports that the infant has never passed meconium within the first 24 hours of life. Despite laxative use, the constipation persists. On examination, the infant has a distended abdomen, and a digital rectal examination reveals an empty rectum with increased anal tone, followed by an explosive discharge of foul-smelling stool and gas upon withdrawal of the finger.

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis given this presentation?
qs.a: The most likely diagnosis is Hirschsprung's disease. The key features supporting this are chronic constipation since birth, delayed meconium passage, abdominal distension, an empty rectum on DRE, and the classic 'squirt sign' (explosive stool and gas upon withdrawal of the finger) which indicates a transition zone.

qs.q: What is the pathophysiology of this condition?
qs.a: Hirschsprung's disease is a congenital disorder characterized by the absence of ganglion cells (aganglionosis) in the myenteric and submucosal plexuses of a segment of the distal bowel, typically the rectum and sigmoid colon. This aganglionic segment fails to relax, leading to a functional obstruction and proximal dilatation of the normally innervated colon.

qs.q: What definitive diagnostic test would you recommend?
qs.a: The definitive diagnostic test for Hirschsprung's disease is a rectal biopsy, which would demonstrate the absence of ganglion cells in the affected bowel segment. Anorectal manometry can also be used to assess the rectoanal inhibitory reflex, which is typically absent in Hirschsprung's disease.

mistakes: Misinterpreting the Rome IV criteria for functional constipation, especially regarding stool size or duration.
Failing to differentiate between functional constipation and organic causes, particularly missing red flags.
Prescribing stimulant laxatives as first-line or for long-term management in children without trying osmotic agents first.
Not addressing fecal impaction as the initial step in management when present.
Over-reliance on dietary changes alone for established chronic constipation without laxative therapy.
Incorrectly defining 'hard stool' by specific diameter cut-offs rather than consistency (Bristol type 1-2) or subjective difficulty.
Stating that the 'stool-holding sign' indicates a large fecal mass, instead of being a behavioral sign of withholding.
Suggesting an overly long duration (e.g., >2 weeks) for suspecting fecal impaction in children.
exam: What are the key history questions to ask when evaluating a child with constipation? — Key questions include: onset and duration of symptoms, stool frequency and consistency (use Bristol Stool Chart if possible), presence of pain during defecation, stool size, presence of fecal soiling (encopresis), dietary habits (fluid and fiber intake), toilet training history, any associated symptoms (abdominal pain, distension, poor appetite, weight loss), and previous treatments.

Describe the physical examination steps for a child presenting with constipation. — General observation for distress, growth parameters (weight, height). Abdominal examination: inspection for distension, visible peristalsis; palpation for tenderness, palpable fecal masses (especially in left lower quadrant), organomegaly. Perianal inspection for fissures, skin tags, signs of abuse. Digital rectal examination (DRE) if indicated: assess anal tone, presence and consistency of stool in the rectum, exclude anatomical abnormalities.

A child has severe constipation with faecal impaction. What is the initial management step? — The initial management step for severe constipation with fecal impaction is disimpaction. This typically involves high doses of osmotic laxatives, such as polyethylene glycol, administered orally over several days until the impaction is cleared. In some cases, rectal enemas may be considered, but oral therapy is generally preferred.

What is the difference between functional constipation and Hirschsprung's disease? — Functional constipation is typically acquired, often related to diet, withholding, or painful defecation, and is characterized by normal innervation of the bowel. Hirschsprung's disease is a congenital condition caused by the absence of ganglion cells in a segment of the distal bowel, leading to a functional obstruction and typically presenting with symptoms from birth or early infancy, often with a history of delayed meconium passage.

Why are stimulant laxatives generally avoided for long-term management of paediatric constipation? — Stimulant laxatives are generally avoided for long-term management due to concerns about potential dependency, damage to colonic nerve plexuses with prolonged use, and the risk of electrolyte imbalances. They are typically reserved for short-term use or when osmotic agents alone are insufficient after optimal dosing and adherence.

What are the potential complications of untreated chronic constipation in children? — Potential complications include fecal impaction, encopresis (fecal soiling), anal fissures, haemorrhoids, recurrent abdominal pain, urinary tract infections (due to bladder compression), poor appetite, psychological distress, and significant impact on quality of life and school performance.

How can you differentiate between overflow incontinence (encopresis) and true faecal incontinence? — Overflow incontinence (encopresis) is typically associated with chronic constipation and fecal impaction, where liquid stool leaks around a hard, retained fecal mass. True fecal incontinence, in contrast, is the involuntary passage of stool in the absence of impaction, often due to underlying neurological or anatomical issues affecting sphincter control.

List and explain the management strategies and red flags for gastrointestinal discomforts including constipation and haemorrhoids. — Management for constipation involves disimpaction (if present), maintenance therapy with osmotic laxatives, dietary modifications (increased fiber and fluid), behavioral interventions (toilet training, regular toilet sitting), and addressing associated psychological factors. For haemorrhoids, management includes stool softeners, increased fiber, topical creams, and rarely, surgical intervention. Red flags for GI discomfort include weight loss, rectal bleeding (not due to fissure), severe abdominal pain, delayed meconium passage, persistent vomiting, fever, and failure to thrive, suggesting organic causes.
